evidence.note: Agent sets up a task system then creates ~10 explicit milestones spanning the subsystems (skeleton/health, DB schema, ORM/JSON, markdown, templates, middleware/headers, handlers, job queue, verification) in a sensible dependency-aware order with rough done-signals baked into each task ('so JSON output matches reference keys', 'ensure binary < 40MB').

The shared cross-runtime job queue (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, dead-letter) — the highest-parity-risk shared-state interface per the task — is sequenced second-to-last rather than de-risked early; this is what keeps the plan below the level-8/10 risk-tiered anchor.
Sustained execution: TaskUpdate cycles each milestone in_progress→completed in the planned order, showing the written plan is referenced and tracked across the whole horizon rather than abandoned.

Verification/parity comparison is a single terminal milestone (27); concrete per-milestone parity exit tests are absent, though incremental reference comparisons (headers, posts, feeds, markdown, admin, auth) do occur during execution.
Mid-run activity is within-milestone bug fixes; no new milestones are created as complexity is discovered, so the plan is not revised — falling short of the level-10 self-reshaping anchor.

reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, written-down, dependency-aware milestone breakdown covering all major subsystems in a sensible order with rough done-signals, and referenced/tracked it via TaskUpdate throughout execution — clearly exceeding the level-5 anchor. It stops short of level 8 because the riskiest shared-state interface (the cross-runtime jobs schema) is sequenced late rather than de-risked first, done-checks are rough with parity verification lumped into one terminal milestone rather than concrete per-milestone exit tests, and the plan was never revised as complexity emerged. This places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.
